item.title: Does easier access to alcohol affect road safety? Evidence from Texas municipalities
item.description: We examine whether legalizing local alcohol sales affects traffic safety, exploiting close local option elections in Texas as a quasi-random source of variation. Over 300 Texas cities voted to legalize alcohol sales between 2003 and 2019. Legalization generated large increases in off-premise alcohol licenses (liquor stores and grocery stores) with little change in on-premise establishments, and shifted alcohol sales from bars and restaurants toward retail outlets for home consumption. Despite these large changes in access, we find no meaningful increase in total crashes, DUI crashes, or fatal crashes, and no evidence of spillover effects on neighboring cities. This null result reflects which type of access was expanded: on-premise licenses are positively associated with crash rates while off-premise licenses are not, consistent with bars and restaurants (not retail stores) being the channel through which alcohol access raises traffic risk.

item.title: Science under collective bargaining: How unionization shapes academic labor markets and research productivity
item.description: This project estimates the causal effects of faculty unionization on wages, employment, and research productivity across academic ranks in U.S. higher education, using staggered difference-in-differences designs and state-level variation in collective bargaining and right-to-work laws.

item.title: Legalized Sports Betting and College Performance
item.description: This project estimates the causal impact of legalized sports betting on college students' academic performance and engagement, using quasi-random variation in exposure to live sporting events generated by individual fandom and course-specific academic schedules at Purdue University.
